endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Even where full automation is the operational goal, initial deployment phases should include meaningful review to validate that the system is behaving as expected before reducing oversight.

commentary.bottom_line: One governance framework (CHAI) recommends meaningful human review of agentic AI actions during initial deployment before oversight is reduced, but no supplied study tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and no empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests staged human review of agentic AI, and no study documents harm from relaxing oversight too early. Under GRADE conventions, a single framework statement counts as expert opinion and cannot support a certainty rating. The effect of this practice on error rates or patient outcomes is unknown.

The only endorsement comes from CHAI governance playbooks, which use "should" language and carry no legal force. The supplied materials cite no FDA, ONC, or state statute that requires a staged oversight period for agentic AI. Adoption therefore depends on each organization's internal governance choices.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared staged human review during early agentic AI deployment with immediate reduced oversight. Studies are needed that measure how often reviewers catch erroneous agent actions, how long review must last before error rates stabilize, what staffing burden review imposes, and what performance thresholds should trigger a reduction in oversight.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from current evidence whether an early review period would detect agent errors that fall unevenly on these patients, or how long such review would need to last in settings with fewer staff.
